burdens.description: Show that physical reality has an ultimately personal, transcendent creator rather than being brute, necessary, or grounded impersonally.
burdens.successCriteria: Give a defensible route from features of physical reality to a personal transcendent cause and answer the principal rival-grounding objections raised in the exchange.

burdens.description: Show that classical theism supplies objective meaning and moral obligation in a way the alternatives do not.
burdens.successCriteria: Explain both the grounding and normative authority of meaning and duty, and answer challenges about arbitrariness, coercion, and independently accessible value.

burdens.description: Defend classical-theist epistemic controls against rival mystical and pluralist accounts.
burdens.successCriteria: Provide public or otherwise discriminating grounds for the classical account and identify non-question-begging defeaters for competing experience-based claims.

burdens.speaker: Jessica Frazier
burdens.description: Develop an impersonal or non-dual account of cosmic unity, order, emergence, and value that is not reducible to classical theism.
burdens.successCriteria: State the alternative's explanatory structure and show how it accounts for relevant features without merely renaming them divine.

burdens.speaker: Philip Goff
burdens.description: Defend a consciousness-involving, limited-God alternative that accommodates existence, fine-tuning, mystical experience, and suffering.
burdens.successCriteria: Connect the experience and metaphysics through an intelligible inference, avoid contradiction, and explain how divine limitation addresses suffering.

burdens.speaker: Joe Folley
burdens.description: Challenge the necessity of classical theism for meaning and normativity while maintaining an appropriately agnostic posture on cosmic origins.
burdens.successCriteria: Distinguish kinds of meaning, explain constraints on valuation or obligation, and identify what theistic authority adds without treating uncertainty as a contrary proof.

burdens.description: Test whether the pro case establishes classical theism rather than only some cause, ground, value source, or religious interpretation.
burdens.successCriteria: Expose an unearned inference from shared or ambiguous evidence to the specifically classical-theist conclusion.

sections.title: Cosmic explanation and comparative scope
sections.weightRationale: The motion centrally asks where physical reality came from and which worldview explains it; this section therefore receives the largest weight without treating Craig's enumerated but mostly undeveloped arguments as six separate successes.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.sourceExcerpt: In the course of my philosophical work, I've defended six arguments for God's existence in support of a positive answer to that question. First, God is the best explanation of why anything at all exists rather than just nothing. Second, God is the best explanation of the absolute beginning of the universe at a point in the finite past.
moves.summary: Craig opens a cumulative explanatory case, foregrounding contingency and a finite cosmic beginning as routes to God.
moves.selectionRationale: This is the pro side's central constructive route to the motion, though the live presentation largely lists rather than develops its members.

passA.rationale: The six-part cumulative structure is intelligible and directly addresses the motion, but the live move lists conclusions without exposing the premises, warrants, or rival comparisons needed to establish them. Calling the case powerful and unmatched is therefore substantially stronger than this presentation supports.

evidence.excerpt: I've defended six arguments for God's existence ... First, God is the best explanation of why anything at all exists ... Second, God is the best explanation of the absolute beginning of the universe.

passB.rationale: The move squarely addresses the motion and gives the cumulative case an intelligible outline. Its principal weakness is warrant: naming familiar arguments and referring to published defenses leaves the live audience unable to inspect most inferential bridges. The strong conclusion therefore exceeds what this particular presentation establishes.

evidence.observation: Craig enumerates six best-explanation claims and calls them a powerful cumulative case, but does not state the premises or comparative warrants for most of them in the live opening.
The claim that no comparable atheistic case exists is asserted without an in-debate comparison.

adjudication.rationale: The opening is centrally relevant and provides a recoverable cumulative outline, but listing best-explanation conclusions without their bridges does not directly discharge the cosmic burden. The final relevance score therefore lies in the competent band rather than either Pass A's completion-level score or Pass B's mixed-band score.

finalResolution.rationale: The opening is centrally relevant and provides a recoverable cumulative outline, but listing best-explanation conclusions without their bridges does not directly discharge the cosmic burden. The final relevance score therefore lies in the competent band rather than either Pass A's completion-level score or Pass B's mixed-band score.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.sourceExcerpt: The reality of temporal becoming is more evident to us than the reality of the external world because we sense temporal becoming in the inner life of the mind, the thoughts that succeed one another as well as in the external world. So, that's I think a quite hopeless defeater of the argument against the infinitude of the past to try to appeal to this tenseless theory of time.
moves.summary: Craig defends temporal becoming against a block-universe escape from a finite-past argument.
moves.selectionRationale: This is the clearest live development of one enumerated cosmological premise and answers a consequential objection raised in audience discussion.

passA.rationale: Craig supplies a direct cumulative reply using metaphysical intuition, experienced temporal succession, expansion, and thermodynamics. It materially develops the finite-past line, but the phenomenology of passage does not alone defeat a tenseless ontology, the scientific references remain uncited, and 'hopeless' overstates the result.

evidence.excerpt: The reality of temporal becoming is more evident to us than the reality of the external world ... that's ... a quite hopeless defeater ... to try to appeal to this tenseless theory of time.

passB.rationale: The reply supplies an identifiable epistemic basis for temporal becoming and directly meets the live block-universe challenge. It remains incomplete as a defense of a finite past: the passage does not show why introspected succession rules out a tenseless ontology, and the categorical dismissal is less calibrated than the support warrants. Confidence is medium because the locked response link points to Folley's earlier Kalam discussion while the anchored passage directly answers a later audience objection.

evidence.observation: Craig treats metaphysical intuitions as defeasible evidence rather than requiring a formal contradiction.
He answers the audience's block-universe proposal by appealing to first-person temporal succession and labels the proposed defeater hopeless.

finalResolution.rationale: Round each dimension's Pass A/Pass B mean, then calculate the move score mechanically.

moves.speaker: Jessica Frazier
moves.sourceExcerpt: If we look at everything in the world around us, all these people, we tend to just see the objects, we need to remember to see the connections, the spaces, the continuum, the way in which everything we see is unified in some sense through causes, through space-time relations.
moves.summary: Frazier proposes cosmic unity and relational continuity as a non-classical starting point for explaining reality.
moves.selectionRationale: It supplies a genuine alternative explanatory frame rather than simply denying Craig's conclusion.

passA.rationale: Relational unity is a genuine alternative starting point and avoids simply denying Craig's conclusion. Yet observed connections do not by themselves yield an explanatory ground, modal anchor, or non-dual ontology; the inference remains suggestive and terminologically loose rather than burden-completing.

evidence.excerpt: We need to remember to see the connections, the spaces, the continuum ... everything we see is unified in some sense through causes, through space-time relations.

passB.rationale: The relational frame is a genuine alternative to an object-first picture and is proportionately presented as an invitation rather than a proof. Yet observed connectedness does not by itself explain why the connections exist or establish a non-dual ground, so the move advances the rival framework more than it completes it.

evidence.observation: Frazier points to causal, spatiotemporal, and modal-order relations as evidence of a unified cosmos and invokes Bradley's regress without developing it.
She treats unity, order, and emergence as grounds for regarding reality as extraordinary or divine while leaving the underlying explanatory mechanism open.

adjudication.rationale: The relational-unity proposal is intelligible as a starting frame, but phrases such as 'unified in some sense' leave the ground, modality, and mechanism materially vague. Pass A's clarity score better matches that transcript compression.

finalResolution.rationale: The relational-unity proposal is intelligible as a starting frame, but phrases such as 'unified in some sense' leave the ground, modality, and mechanism materially vague. Pass A's clarity score better matches that transcript compression.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
moves.sourceExcerpt: I'm also very much persuaded by certain traditional arguments for God's existence, kind of like Bill likes, arguments rooted in the need to explain why the universe exists, why it's fine-tuned for life. The problem is though, I'm also completely persuaded by the most discussed argument against God's existence rooted in the need to explain why there's so much suffering in the world.
moves.summary: Goff accepts explanatory arguments toward God but argues that suffering counts against the classical package.
moves.selectionRationale: This defines his alternative's comparative burden and prevents agreement on cosmological data from being mistaken for agreement on classical theism.

passA.rationale: Goff fairly grants the explanatory pressure toward God while isolating suffering as evidence against the classical package. This is a clear comparative constraint, but neither the positive arguments nor the suffering likelihoods are developed here, so the move frames rather than resolves the comparison.

evidence.excerpt: I'm ... persuaded by certain traditional arguments for God's existence ... The problem is ... I'm also completely persuaded by ... the need to explain why there's so much suffering in the world.

passB.rationale: This is a clear and unusually charitable comparative move: it preserves the force of the pro evidence while denying that it secures an all-powerful classical God. Its score is limited because the suffering premise and the limited-God reconciliation are announced rather than developed into a predictive or explanatory model.

evidence.observation: Goff expressly grants that cosmological and fine-tuning considerations favor God, then sets suffering against the classical package.
He proposes divine limitation as the solution but supplies only the assertion that God made the best universe possible.

finalResolution.rationale: Round each dimension's Pass A/Pass B mean, then calculate the move score mechanically.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.sourceExcerpt: There's an attempt to use principles that are considered to be justified in order to trace something in the Kalam case, trace something back to the beginning of the universe and infer something about it. And then through the second stage we establish that cause has various properties and it begins to look like God.
moves.summary: Folley grants the Kalam's intelligible two-stage structure while questioning extrapolation from in-universe causal principles.
moves.selectionRationale: The concession and bounded objection accurately represent his agnostic role and directly test the pro inference.

passA.rationale: Folley reconstructs the two-stage Kalam charitably, concedes its intelligibility, and targets the transfer of causal principles from ordinary objects beyond the universe. The challenge is well located but remains compressed: it does not specify which causal warrant fails or how that affects each second-stage property.

evidence.excerpt: There's a sort of like two-step process ... trace something back to the beginning of the universe ... And then through the second stage we establish that cause has various properties and it begins to look like God.

passB.rationale: Folley accurately reconstructs the argument before locating the contested extrapolation, which makes the challenge responsive and fair. The objection is not fully defended with a positive account of which causal principles fail or why, but its deliberately bounded conclusion suits his agnostic burden and tests a decisive bridge.

evidence.observation: Folley reconstructs the Kalam as a first-stage causal inference followed by a second-stage attribution of divine properties.
He identifies his reservation as exporting causal principles from middle-sized, in-universe cases while still calling the argument intelligible and partly compelling.

finalResolution.rationale: Round each dimension's Pass A/Pass B mean, then calculate the move score mechanically.

sections.title: Creator, creation, and non-dual alternatives
sections.weightRationale: The exchange directly tests whether explanatory dependence entails ontological separation, emanation, or overlap, an important discriminator among the represented worldviews.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.sourceExcerpt: There's a creator-creation distinction since the creation is material in space and time, but the creator is an immaterial, spiritual, transcendent reality that has brought the physical world into being. In this case, we would want to say, I think, that God is what you've called a self-natured being.
moves.summary: Craig distinguishes a necessary immaterial creator from contingent material creation rather than treating both as one substance.
moves.selectionRationale: It states the classical ontology required for the pro conclusion and directly contrasts with Frazier's grounding language.

passA.rationale: Craig clearly states the classical distinction and later specifies necessary creator versus contingent universe, directly answering Frazier's leveling move. The ontology is coherent as a model, but the move mainly defines the view; it does not independently establish that this creator exists or is personal.

evidence.excerpt: There's a creator-creation distinction since the creation is material in space and time, but the creator is an immaterial, spiritual, transcendent reality that has brought the physical world into being.

passB.rationale: Craig states the classical ontology precisely and directly distinguishes causal dependence from material composition. The move substantially advances the pro burden, but it assumes rather than demonstrates that physical reality is wholly contingent and that the necessary source is personal, leaving important motion-level bridges outside this exchange.

evidence.observation: Craig separates an immaterial, necessary creator from contingent material creation and secures partial agreement about the necessary/contingent distinction.

finalResolution.rationale: Round each dimension's Pass A/Pass B mean, then calculate the move score mechanically.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.sourceExcerpt: If one circle of the Venn diagram represents everything that is timeless, immaterial, spaceless, necessarily existent, and the other circle represents everything that is temporal, material, contingent, then they cannot overlap. Those are self-contradictory. So, the area of overlap is a contradiction.
moves.summary: Craig argues that Goff's proposed overlap combines mutually exclusive modal and physical properties.
moves.selectionRationale: This is a direct, premise-level objection to the most distinctive con metaphysical proposal.

passA.rationale: Given Craig's exhaustive property assignments, non-overlap follows clearly and directly tests Goff's centerpiece. But the objection treats the whole universe as essentially temporal, material, and contingent before Goff has granted that classification; calling the overlap itself contradictory is therefore too quick rather than decisive.

evidence.excerpt: If one circle ... represents everything that is timeless, immaterial, spaceless, necessarily existent, and the other ... temporal, material, contingent, then they cannot overlap.

passB.rationale: The incompatibility inference is coherent under Craig's stipulated property sets. Its weakness is responsiveness: Goff had not conceded that every aspect of the universe is essentially temporal and contingent, so the objection partly builds the contradiction into a characterization the target can reject. The categorical conclusion is therefore less charitable than the conditional success warrants.

evidence.observation: Craig defines one circle by timeless, immaterial, necessary properties and the other by temporal, material, contingent properties, then infers that their overlap would be contradictory.
Goff immediately denies that the entire physical universe belongs to Craig's contingent-property set.

adjudication.rationale: Craig's contradiction follows under his two exhaustive property sets, but Goff had located a necessary, timeless conscious core within the universe and immediately rejected the claim that the whole universe is essentially contingent. The objection therefore attacks a characterization the target did not accept; Pass B correctly places responsiveness in the weaker-reconstruction band.

finalResolution.rationale: Craig's contradiction follows under his two exhaustive property sets, but Goff had located a necessary, timeless conscious core within the universe and immediately rejected the claim that the whole universe is essentially contingent. The objection therefore attacks a characterization the target did not accept; Pass B correctly places responsiveness in the weaker-reconstruction band.

moves.speaker: Jessica Frazier
moves.sourceExcerpt: There's whatever creates the world. If you're a Thomist, they're the powers in God, the concepts in God that unfold and generate. And then there's the parts of God which are under it. And if you're a physicist, there's the Big Bang and the whatever it is that's generating space-time.
moves.summary: Frazier argues that traditions commonly distinguish the manifested world's generative level from an inaccessible supporting condition.
moves.selectionRationale: This gives substantive metaphysical content to her claim that classical creation is not the only two-level account.

passA.rationale: The cross-tradition comparison usefully shows that two-level dependence accounts are not unique to classical creation. However, 'under,' 'surrounding,' and 'supporting' are left metaphorical, and grouping Thomism, Kabbalah, and physics does not establish a common causal structure or a superior non-dual model.

evidence.excerpt: There's whatever creates the world ... And then there's the parts of God which are under it ... there's the Big Bang and ... whatever it is that's generating space-time.

passB.rationale: The move usefully shifts the comparison from creation versus no creation to competing accounts of generative and supporting levels. Its categories remain loose: physical antecedents, divine concepts, and ontological grounds are grouped without showing that they perform the same explanatory role, so it opens an alternative more clearly than it establishes one.

evidence.observation: Frazier compares Thomistic powers, the Big Bang, and inaccessible supporting conditions as versions of a two-level account.

finalResolution.rationale: Round each dimension's Pass A/Pass B mean, then calculate the move score mechanically.

moves.speaker: Jessica Frazier
moves.sourceExcerpt: Emanationism gets given lots of different ontological sort of play outs, right? I mean, even Aquinas will say creation ex nihilo never means that God creates the world and then he's like, ‘That was great. I'm going away.’ In fact, that was a heresy. The universe, all that the divine creates, is always sustained.
moves.summary: Frazier emphasizes continuous divine sustaining to narrow the alleged contrast between creation and emanation.
moves.selectionRationale: This is a direct reply showing shared dependence language while preserving disagreement about ontological interpretation.

passA.rationale: Frazier accurately narrows the disagreement by distinguishing classical creation from deism and emphasizing continuous dependence. This directly blocks an exaggerated contrast with emanation, though shared sustaining language does not erase the remaining disagreement over identity, contingency, and creation from no material substrate.

evidence.excerpt: Creation ex nihilo never means that God creates the world and then he's like, 'That was great. I'm going away.' ... The universe ... is always sustained.

passB.rationale: The reply directly narrows an overstated contrast without claiming that sustaining and emanation are identical. It is well targeted and historically specific, though it does not eliminate Craig's residual distinction between creation by God and creation out of God, so it earns a strong rather than decisive score.

evidence.observation: Frazier correctly distinguishes deistic abandonment from continuous sustaining and argues that both creation and emanation can involve ongoing dependence.
Craig preserves the remaining difference by explaining Aquinas's creation event and creation not out of anything.

finalResolution.rationale: Round each dimension's Pass A/Pass B mean, then calculate the move score mechanically.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
moves.sourceExcerpt: Think of a Venn diagram where you've got the bit of God that's wholly other, that's completely separate from the universe; the bit of the universe or the nature of the universe which is wholly separate to God; and then the bit in the middle, like a Venn diagram.
moves.summary: Goff proposes partial overlap between God and universe, with pure consciousness occupying their shared necessary core.
moves.selectionRationale: This is the distinctive metaphysical centerpiece of his alternative and invites the debate's clearest internal-coherence challenge.

passA.rationale: The overlap model is relevant and recoverable, and it offers a genuine alternative to strict separation and identity. Initially, however, the shared property's modal and physical status is unspecified and supported mainly by Goff's experience, leaving the central overlap vulnerable to exactly the coherence challenge Craig raises.

evidence.excerpt: Think of a Venn diagram where you've got the bit of God that's wholly other ... the bit of the universe ... wholly separate to God; and then the bit in the middle.

passB.rationale: The Venn model is understandable and directly proposes a third option between strict separation and identity. At this stage, however, the overlap is supported primarily by Goff's interpretation of his experience; the modal status and membership conditions of the purported necessary conscious core remain asserted rather than independently warranted.

evidence.observation: Goff places pure consciousness in an overlap between God and universe, contrasting this with both strict creator separation and pantheistic identity.

finalResolution.rationale: Round each dimension's Pass A/Pass B mean, then calculate the move score mechanically.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
moves.sourceExcerpt: I wouldn't define the physical universe as essentially contingent then. I think most of it is, but I think there's something at the core of the universe, there's something at the core of you, Bill, and at the core of me that is necessary, timeless, uncreated. And that's where the overlap is.
moves.summary: Goff rejects Craig's definition of the entire universe as contingent and locates overlap in a necessary conscious core.
moves.selectionRationale: It directly answers the contradiction charge by revising the property assignment rather than accepting Craig's two-circle setup.

passA.rationale: Goff answers the formal contradiction by rejecting Craig's exhaustive property assignment and locating the overlap only in a necessary conscious core. That is a logically available repair, but the existence and relation of this core to the physical universe remain asserted rather than independently warranted.

evidence.excerpt: I wouldn't define the physical universe as essentially contingent ... there's something at the core ... that is necessary, timeless, uncreated. And that's where the overlap is.

passB.rationale: This is a direct premise-level answer to Craig's contradiction charge and makes the proposed overlap logically possible by revising the relevant classification. It establishes compatibility, not probability: Goff still offers little public warrant that such a core exists or belongs both to persons and to God.

evidence.observation: Goff explicitly rejects essential contingency for the whole universe and restricts the overlap to a timeless, necessary, uncreated conscious core.

finalResolution.rationale: Round each dimension's Pass A/Pass B mean, then calculate the move score mechanically.

sections.title: Mystical experience and public warrant
sections.weightRationale: Mystical experience supplies Goff's principal evidence and generates sustained replies about cognitive content, defeaters, and public accessibility; it is tied with cosmic explanation for highest weight.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.sourceExcerpt: Once one starts appealing to these sorts of mystical experiences to justify your worldview, it seems to me that you've lost all controls on objectivity and on truth. I too could claim what you would probably call a mystical experience, namely, at the age of sixteen, after six months of the most intense soul-searching I've ever been through, I was spiritually born again.
moves.summary: Craig challenges private mystical evidence as lacking objective controls and contrasts it with his Christian experience.
moves.selectionRationale: It raises the debate's primary discriminating-evidence objection to Goff's experiential case.

passA.rationale: Craig directly raises the rival-experience and discriminating-control problem, then identifies public historical evidence as the kind of control he thinks is needed. The challenge is strong, but his resurrection warrant is only asserted in this debate and his language initially risks treating all private experience as evidentially uncontrolled.

evidence.excerpt: Once one starts appealing to these sorts of mystical experiences to justify your worldview ... you've lost all controls on objectivity and on truth. I too could claim ... a mystical experience.

passB.rationale: Craig identifies the decisive epistemic issue—how rival experiences are discriminated—and fairly acknowledges that he also relies on experience. His proposed external control is relevant, yet merely referring to historical reasons does not demonstrate their quality here, and the suspicion of Goff can apply reciprocally unless the asserted control is supplied.

evidence.observation: Craig raises the need for truth controls and introduces his own Christian experience as a rival interpretation class.
He claims historical resurrection evidence controls the Christian experience, but does not present that evidence in this exchange.

finalResolution.rationale: Round each dimension's Pass A/Pass B mean, then calculate the move score mechanically.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.sourceExcerpt: How do you know, Philip, that your mystical experience was not an experience of the orthodox God? How do you know that it was this indescribable, self-contradictory, strange God, especially since there doesn't seem to be any cognitive content to differentiate it? Maybe you had an experience of the orthodox God.
moves.summary: Craig argues that Goff lacks content capable of discriminating his interpretation from an orthodox theistic one.
moves.selectionRationale: This targets the underdetermination of worldview by the reported experience rather than denying the experience occurred.

passA.rationale: Craig targets the decisive underdetermination: an ineffable or minimally structured experience lacks resources to select Goff's limited, overlapping God over orthodox theism. The challenge is direct and proportionate as an epistemic defeater, though calling Goff's God self-contradictory imports the still-disputed ontology from the previous exchange.

evidence.excerpt: How do you know ... your mystical experience was not an experience of the orthodox God? ... there doesn't seem to be any cognitive content to differentiate it.

passB.rationale: Craig targets underdetermination rather than merely denying that the experience occurred, directly pressing Goff's strongest evidential bridge. The challenge is highly relevant and survives the immediate answer because non-differentiation does not select all the further theological properties. Calling the rival view strange and self-contradictory is unnecessary overstatement, which restrains calibration.

evidence.observation: Craig asks what content distinguishes Goff's limited or overlap interpretation from an orthodox-God interpretation.
Goff replies that the lack of self/other differentiation belongs to the experience, but offers no independent criterion selecting the broader limited-God package.

adjudication.rationale: The underdetermination challenge directly reaches Goff's strongest evidential bridge. Calling the rival view strange and self-contradictory imports a still-disputed characterization, however, so Pass B's lower calibration score is warranted without weakening the core objection.

finalResolution.rationale: The underdetermination challenge directly reaches Goff's strongest evidential bridge. Calling the rival view strange and self-contradictory imports a still-disputed characterization, however, so Pass B's lower calibration score is warranted without weakening the core objection.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
moves.sourceExcerpt: Neurophysiologically, what it looks like it's doing is suppressing, stopping neural activity, not creating new neural activity like you imagine in a hallucination. Imagine my mind is a light bulb wrapped in cotton wool. The cotton wool is what's particular to me, Philip Goff, and the light bulb is this pure consciousness.
moves.summary: Goff uses neural suppression and a filter metaphor to interpret ego dissolution as disclosure rather than fabrication.
moves.selectionRationale: This is the main warrant connecting the drug-induced experience to his consciousness-first metaphysics.

passA.rationale: Neural suppression is relevant to the simple claim that the drug merely adds ordinary hallucinatory imagery, and the filter metaphor makes Goff's interpretation intelligible. Yet reduced activity does not itself discriminate disclosure from distortion, while the neurophysiological claim and pure-consciousness bridge are not documented.

evidence.excerpt: Neurophysiologically ... it's doing is suppressing, stopping neural activity, not creating new neural activity like you imagine in a hallucination ... the light bulb is this pure consciousness.

passB.rationale: The move supplies an intelligible filter hypothesis and connects the experience to Goff's consciousness-first account. But neural suppression is asserted without presented data, and reduced activity does not itself discriminate disclosure from disruption or hallucination. The metaphor therefore carries more inferential weight than the live evidence supports.

evidence.observation: Goff says the drug suppresses neural activity and uses a light-bulb/filter metaphor to interpret the experience as disclosure.
He acknowledges that the experience alone would fit Brahman and imports purpose from a separate account of God's essence.

adjudication.rationale: Neural suppression and the filter metaphor make Goff's interpretation intelligible and materially relevant, but neither discriminates disclosure from disruption. The move advances the burden without completing it, and its central metaphor remains clearer than Pass A allowed but less precise than Pass B suggested.

finalResolution.rationale: Neural suppression and the filter metaphor make Goff's interpretation intelligible and materially relevant, but neither discriminates disclosure from disruption. The move advances the burden without completing it, and its central metaphor remains clearer than Pass A allowed but less precise than Pass B suggested.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
moves.sourceExcerpt: You can't get outside of your consciousness and check whether it's corresponding to reality. So, what do you do? You've just got to decide which experiences seem most evident. And anybody who's had the experience I had—it is more compelling than anything in ordinary experience, far more compelling. Also, with this particular substance, it is very uniform.
moves.summary: Goff argues that all knowledge begins from apparent experience and cites intensity and uniformity as support.
moves.selectionRationale: This is his direct epistemic response to the demand for external verification.

passA.rationale: The appeal to experiential starting points answers the demand for impossible Cartesian certainty, and claimed cross-subject uniformity is relevant. It does not answer the live asymmetry in defeaters, practical indispensability, or public checkability; intensity and felt certainty alone provide a weak bridge to Goff's metaphysical interpretation.

evidence.excerpt: You can't get outside of your consciousness and check whether it's corresponding to reality ... decide which experiences seem most evident ... it is more compelling than anything in ordinary experience.

passB.rationale: The reply directly challenges selective skepticism and adds intensity and uniformity as possible reliability indicators. It does not answer the central rival-hypothesis problem: ordinary perception's practical, intersubjective, and predictive controls may differ from a drug-induced state, and compelling seeming alone is not a discriminating warrant.

evidence.observation: Goff argues that all knowledge begins with trusted experience and cites exceptional vividness and cross-user uniformity.
He concedes the possibility of delusion but says phenomenal force justifies trust.

adjudication.rationale: The reply clearly identifies intensity and cross-subject uniformity as proposed reliability indicators. Its failure is not opacity but the weak warrant from compelling seeming to a discriminating metaphysical interpretation, so Pass B's clarity score is better placed.

finalResolution.rationale: The reply clearly identifies intensity and cross-subject uniformity as proposed reliability indicators. Its failure is not opacity but the weak warrant from compelling seeming to a discriminating metaphysical interpretation, so Pass B's clarity score is better placed.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.sourceExcerpt: I don't quite know what an unstructured cognitive content looks like. It seems like the really cool thing and the useful thing about cognitive content is that we can put it in structures and thus it can enter the public arena of discourse. It seems like cognitive content, at least as far as I can tell, would imply structure.
moves.summary: Folley questions whether purportedly unstructured content can support publicly assessable inferences.
moves.selectionRationale: This preserves intra-side disagreement and isolates a key gap between private seeming and third-party warrant.

passA.rationale: Folley isolates the tension between content said to be unstructured and content capable of supporting public inference, while later distinguishing indispensable hinge commitments from dispensable mystical beliefs. He frames the objection tentatively and accurately; the pragmatic criterion is defended conceptually rather than demonstrated as exhaustive.

evidence.excerpt: I don't quite know what an unstructured cognitive content looks like ... cognitive content ... can enter the public arena of discourse ... would imply structure.

passB.rationale: Folley isolates both the conceptual problem in 'unstructured content' and a relevant difference between mystical experience and indispensable background commitments. The challenge is precise, direct, and modestly framed as uncertainty rather than refutation. Its evidential component is philosophical rather than empirical, but that is appropriate to the inference tested.

evidence.observation: Folley asks how content can be cognitive yet unstructured and links structure to entry into public discourse.
He distinguishes indispensable hinge commitments from spiritual experiences that can be discarded while ordinary action continues.

finalResolution.rationale: Round each dimension's Pass A/Pass B mean, then calculate the move score mechanically.

moves.speaker: Jessica Frazier
moves.sourceExcerpt: You might have to speak to experiences that go beyond the usual. The first time as a kid I experienced what it was like when the plane dives and you feel weightlessness, it was a new experience. It didn't mean it was not a veridical experience. It was just an unusual thing.
moves.summary: Frazier argues that unfamiliar phenomenology is not by itself evidence of fabrication or non-veridicality.
moves.selectionRationale: It offers a limited defense of unusual experience without fully endorsing Goff's metaphysical interpretation.

passA.rationale: The weightlessness analogy correctly shows that novelty or unfamiliar phenomenology is not by itself a defeater, and Frazier limits the conclusion accordingly. The analogy does not establish that a drug-induced experience tracks an external metaphysical object or that Goff's interpretation is the best one.

evidence.excerpt: The first time as a kid I experienced ... weightlessness, it was a new experience. It didn't mean it was not a veridical experience. It was just an unusual thing.

passB.rationale: The analogy successfully defeats a crude inference from unfamiliarity to non-veridicality and is carefully limited. It does not establish that a pharmacologically induced experience accurately reveals a necessary conscious ground, so it repairs one vulnerability in Goff's case without supplying the missing positive discriminator.

evidence.observation: Frazier uses an unfamiliar but veridical weightlessness experience to show that unusual phenomenology does not entail fabrication.
She explicitly leaves admissibility as evidence open rather than claiming the experience proves Goff's metaphysics.

finalResolution.rationale: Round each dimension's Pass A/Pass B mean, then calculate the move score mechanically.

sections.title: Objective and subjective meaning
sections.weightRationale: Meaning is explicit in the motion and opening cases, but the discussion concerns several distinct senses and is less directly developed than origins or mystical warrant.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.sourceExcerpt: Many atheists have recognized that if God does not exist, then our lives are ultimately meaningless. For no matter what we do, it really doesn't matter because everything winds up the same regardless. You can try to make up a meaning to your life, but that's purely subjective. That's just pretending that your life has meaning.
moves.summary: Craig argues that temporal extinction makes self-created meaning objectively insignificant despite subjective fulfillment.
moves.selectionRationale: This is the pro side's main meaning argument and sets the distinction contested by all three opposing speakers.

passA.rationale: The move clearly identifies ultimate objective significance as the pro burden and connects it to divine purpose. But universal extinction does not by itself entail that present acts lack objective importance, and calling subject-involving meaning mere pretending dismisses alternatives before supplying the needed bridge.

evidence.excerpt: If God does not exist, then our lives are ultimately meaningless ... You can try to make up a meaning ... but that's purely subjective. That's just pretending.

passB.rationale: The move clearly frames the pro burden and connects temporal permanence to one recognizable sense of ultimate significance. The missing bridge is material: it does not show why later extinction cancels present relational or evaluative facts, or why subject-involving meaning is unreal. Labeling alternatives as pretending also weakens charity.

evidence.observation: Craig infers from eventual cosmic extinction that present actions objectively lack significance and characterizes constructed meaning as pretending.
He contrasts this with everlasting significance under a Christian afterlife.

adjudication.rationale: The opening clearly frames one recognizable kind of ultimate significance and is directly burden-relevant. It does not supply the bridge from eventual extinction to present objective insignificance and dismisses subject-involving meaning as pretense, so the final result remains in the mixed band.

finalResolution.rationale: The opening clearly frames one recognizable kind of ultimate significance and is directly burden-relevant. It does not supply the bridge from eventual extinction to present objective insignificance and dismisses subject-involving meaning as pretense, so the final result remains in the mixed band.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.sourceExcerpt: I'm talking about meaning in an objective sense, not a subjective sense. Is there an objective meaning to human existence? And it seems to me to have an objective meaning, we need this external transcendent reality, God, to tell us what the objective meaning in life is. The meaning of life is to glorify God and to know him and enjoy him forever.
moves.summary: Craig clarifies that his claim concerns objective human purpose grounded in a transcendent divine source.
moves.selectionRationale: This is the explicit burden clarification, though it precedes rather than fully answers Frazier's worthiness objection.

passA.rationale: Craig usefully clarifies that his target is objective human purpose and states the Christian candidate precisely. The claim that such purpose needs a transcendent personal source is asserted rather than argued, and the move does not answer the later distinction between assignment, authority, and worthiness.

evidence.excerpt: I'm talking about meaning in an objective sense ... we need this external transcendent reality, God, to tell us what the objective meaning in life is.

passB.rationale: The clarification is precise and directly answers Folley's focus on subjective senses. It nevertheless asserts both that objective meaning requires God and that God's stated end is worthy without an argument for either bridge. Because it precedes and does not later answer the creator-versus-value objection, it advances but does not complete the burden.

evidence.observation: Craig explicitly defines his target as objective human purpose and identifies glorifying and knowing God as that purpose.
Frazier's ensuing objection shows that external assignment and evaluative worth remain distinct.

adjudication.rationale: Craig precisely states the proposed objective purpose and directly clarifies his target, but he asserts rather than defends the need for a transcendent assigner and the worthiness of the assigned end. The move materially advances rather than completes the locked burden.

finalResolution.rationale: Craig precisely states the proposed objective purpose and directly clarifies his target, but he asserts rather than defends the need for a transcendent assigner and the worthiness of the assigned end. The move materially advances rather than completes the locked burden.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.sourceExcerpt: We hear ‘what is the meaning of life’ and we are necessarily fixed into a kind of reified view of the question. We think, ‘Okay, there must be this thing called meaning out there and we need to find it.’ If we look at the way that we use the term meaning, it seems to refer to different related but ultimately distinct things.
moves.summary: Folley rejects a single reified meaning-property and distinguishes several ordinary senses of meaningfulness.
moves.selectionRationale: It directly challenges the pro argument's unitary objective-versus-subjective framing.

passA.rationale: Folley directly exposes the unitary treatment of meaning as a linguistic and conceptual assumption, then distinguishes fulfillment, aim, sacrifice, and duration. He charitably grants that afterlife can improve some senses. The usage-based warrant is persuasive but does not by itself settle whether an additional objective-purpose property exists.

evidence.excerpt: We hear 'what is the meaning of life' ... there must be this thing called meaning ... If we look at the way that we use the term meaning, it seems to refer to different related but ultimately distinct things.

passB.rationale: The analysis directly exposes equivocation in the pro side's unitary objective/subjective contrast and supports the distinction with concrete cases. Folley's concessions prevent the taxonomy from becoming a denial by definition. The account remains partly programmatic, but it materially reframes the burden in a more auditable way.

evidence.observation: Folley challenges reification of a single meaning-property and separates related senses of meaningfulness.
He tests duration, fulfillment, effort, sacrifice, and psychological disposition as distinct dimensions, conceding that theism can improve some of them.

finalResolution.rationale: Round each dimension's Pass A/Pass B mean, then calculate the move score mechanically.

moves.speaker: Jessica Frazier
moves.sourceExcerpt: If God says, ‘What I really want you to do is kick puppies, and if you do it really well, you'll get to heaven,’ your job is to say, ‘That's stupid. Even though you're God and you created me, I'm not going to do that. I have access to higher values.’ Just because you're created for something doesn't mean you have to value it.
moves.summary: Frazier argues that being created for a purpose does not itself make that purpose worthy of endorsement.
moves.selectionRationale: This exposes the missing bridge from creator-given telos to objectively valuable meaning.

passA.rationale: The counterexample cleanly separates being assigned a purpose from that purpose's worthiness, exposing a missing evaluative bridge in creator-grounded meaning. It is a strong conceptual defeater of the bare inference, although it does not show that a necessarily good creator's actual purpose would be defective.

evidence.excerpt: Even though you're God and you created me, I'm not going to do that. I have access to higher values. Just because you're created for something doesn't mean you have to value it.

passB.rationale: The counterexample directly identifies the missing normativity bridge from creator-given purpose to worthwhile purpose. It does not prove that the classical God could prescribe cruelty, but it need not: it shows that authorship alone is insufficient unless the pro case also establishes the creator's goodness and the worth of the assigned end.

evidence.observation: Frazier's harmful-purpose counterexample separates being created for an end from having reason to value that end.

finalResolution.rationale: Round each dimension's Pass A/Pass B mean, then calculate the move score mechanically.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.sourceExcerpt: It's clearly not arbitrary in the sense that you can't choose to find anything meaningful. Even if we take a radically extreme subjectivist position on meaning, there are still broad limitations on what you can create. If you're a naturalist, then there are still going to be a limited number of things that most humans would be able to value.
moves.summary: Folley argues that subject-involving meaning remains constrained by psychology and is not freely or infinitely arbitrary.
moves.selectionRationale: It directly answers Craig's claim that constructed meaning is merely arbitrary while avoiding a stronger stance-independent claim.

passA.rationale: Folley directly rebuts the equation of subject-involving meaning with unconstrained choice by appealing to stable psychological and species-level limits. He carefully allows unacceptable values within those limits. The account constrains valuation but does not yet supply an interpersonal standard for adjudicating conflicts.

evidence.excerpt: It's clearly not arbitrary in the sense that you can't choose to find anything meaningful ... even ... a radically extreme subjectivist position ... there are still broad limitations on what you can create.

passB.rationale: The reply effectively rebuts the claim that constructed meaning is freely or infinitely arbitrary and calibrates its conclusion with an explicit concession. Psychological constraint does not by itself yield objective worth or resolve conflicts among possible meanings, so the move supports a bounded naturalistic answer rather than a complete normative theory.

evidence.observation: Folley argues that even radical subjectivism is constrained by human psychology and openly concedes that unacceptable options can remain within those limits.

finalResolution.rationale: Round each dimension's Pass A/Pass B mean, then calculate the move score mechanically.

sections.title: Moral value, obligation, and authority
sections.weightRationale: Objective moral obligation is one of Craig's six stated arguments and receives extended, direct engagement about value, oughtness, prudence, and authority.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.sourceExcerpt: Objectivity is not enough by itself to have objective moral values. We need some sort of oughtness: I ought to do this; I ought not to do that. This is a matter of moral duties. Moral duties arise from imperatives issued by a qualified authority. And God, as the paradigmatic good, is qualified to issue such moral commands to us.
moves.summary: Craig grounds values in God's good nature and duties in commands from a qualified authority.
moves.selectionRationale: This is the pro side's most explicit inferential account of moral obligation and directly develops Folley's distinction.

passA.rationale: Craig directly develops Folley's distinction by separating value grounded in divine nature from duty grounded in commands of a qualified authority. The model is clear and highly burden-relevant, but the authority-to-obligation bridge and God's qualification are stated rather than defended against arbitrariness or independent-value objections.

evidence.excerpt: Moral duties arise from imperatives issued by a qualified authority. And God, as the paradigmatic good, is qualified to issue such moral commands to us.

passB.rationale: Craig provides the section's clearest positive account of both value and oughtness and directly develops Folley's distinction. The material unresolved bridge is why commands from even a paradigmatically good creator constitute obligations for other agents, rather than reliable advice or powerful demands; qualification is asserted more than defended.

evidence.observation: Craig separates values grounded in God's good nature from duties generated by commands of a qualified authority.

adjudication.rationale: This is the section's clearest positive model and directly distinguishes value from duty. The unresolved authority-to-obligation bridge prevents a very-strong score, while its precision and directness support a result above Pass B's lower edge.

finalResolution.rationale: This is the section's clearest positive model and directly distinguishes value from duty. The unresolved authority-to-obligation bridge prevents a very-strong score, while its precision and directness support a result above Pass B's lower edge.

moves.speaker: William Lane Craig
moves.sourceExcerpt: What happens when your moral duty contradicts what prudence tells you to do? Self-interest and morality often come head-on into conflict. Theism provides a basis for doing your moral duty even at the expense of self-interest, and therefore following your moral obligations over your prudential interests. That's one more practical argument in support of a theistic perspective.
moves.summary: Craig distinguishes moral duty from prudence and argues that theism supports duty when self-interest conflicts.
moves.selectionRationale: This directly resists Folley's tendency to identify theism's moral force with reward, punishment, or prudential alignment.

passA.rationale: Craig correctly distinguishes moral duty from prudence and directly resists Folley's reduction of theism's force to reward and punishment. The move clarifies the target, but saying theism supplies the basis does not show why divine grounding succeeds or why non-theistic duty cannot override self-interest.

evidence.excerpt: What happens when your moral duty contradicts what prudence tells you to do? ... Theism provides a basis for doing your moral duty even at the expense of self-interest.

passB.rationale: The response correctly resists reducing morality to prudence and directly engages Folley's enforcement framing. It does not explain how theism produces non-prudential compliance rather than adding afterlife incentives or authoritative commands, so the claimed practical advantage remains underwarranted despite a clear distinction.

evidence.observation: Craig distinguishes moral duty from self-interest and claims theism grounds adherence when the two conflict.
Folley's immediately preceding position concerned divine power making compliance prudential, so Craig directly identifies the distinction at issue.

adjudication.rationale: Craig correctly separates duty from prudence and directly answers Folley's enforcement framing. Saying theism supplies a basis does not explain non-prudential authority or exclude non-theistic duty, so the move is competent and responsive but incomplete.

finalResolution.rationale: Craig correctly separates duty from prudence and directly answers Folley's enforcement framing. Saying theism supplies a basis does not explain non-prudential authority or exclude non-theistic duty, so the move is competent and responsive but incomplete.

moves.speaker: Jessica Frazier
moves.sourceExcerpt: Hinduism says there are moral structures. If you're in the world and you're a consciousness and you're interacting with other consciousness, you have moral responsibilities. And since you are and I am and we all are here, we have those responsibilities. Hinduism is extremely invested in understanding what's called dharma, the structure of how the world around us works.
moves.summary: Frazier grounds moral responsibility in conscious interaction and dharmic structure rather than divine punishment.
moves.selectionRationale: This corrects a live characterization of Hinduism and supplies a positive rival account of obligation.

passA.rationale: Frazier directly corrects the claim that Hinduism lacks obligation and offers conscious interaction, pain, and dharmic structure as a rival ground. The account is relevant and positive, but the inference from interaction or painfulness to categorical responsibility is mostly asserted rather than developed.

evidence.excerpt: If you're ... a consciousness and you're interacting with other consciousness, you have moral responsibilities ... Hinduism is ... invested in ... dharma, the structure of how the world around us works.

passB.rationale: Frazier corrects the live characterization of Hinduism and offers a positive rival basis in conscious interaction, suffering, and dharmic order. The account remains compressed: it does not fully derive categorical duties from those facts or explain why dharmic structure has authority, so it is a useful but incomplete alternative.

evidence.observation: Frazier grounds responsibility in interaction among conscious beings and in dharmic structure rather than divine punishment.
She adds that the character of pain supplies a reason for prevention and distinguishes morality from fear of punishment.

adjudication.rationale: Frazier directly corrects the characterization of Hinduism and offers conscious interaction and dharmic order as a positive rival basis. The categorical-authority bridge is compressed, so the move strongly advances but does not discharge its burden.

finalResolution.rationale: Frazier directly corrects the characterization of Hinduism and offers conscious interaction and dharmic order as a positive rival basis. The categorical-authority bridge is compressed, so the move strongly advances but does not discharge its burden.

moves.speaker: Joe Folley
moves.sourceExcerpt: The mere objectivity of value seems to be underselling the strength of theism here. The Platonic good is a little bit toothless. The advantage of theism isn't necessarily in the mere objectivity of values. It's in the presence of an enforcer of values. That doesn't have anything to do with objectivity at all.
moves.summary: Folley distinguishes objective value from the prudential force supplied by a powerful divine enforcer.
moves.selectionRationale: This concedes a practical advantage to theism while challenging whether it establishes genuinely objective morality.

passA.rationale: Folley sharply distinguishes stance-independent value from the prudential force of an enforcing agent, while conceding theism's practical advantage. This accurately exposes a live ambiguity between moral authority and power, though it does not yet explain non-theistic categorical obligation.

evidence.excerpt: The advantage of theism isn't necessarily in the mere objectivity of values. It's in the presence of an enforcer of values. That doesn't have anything to do with objectivity at all.

passB.rationale: The move draws a consequential distinction between truth, normative authority, motivation, and enforcement while granting theism a practical advantage. It somewhat compresses the difference between a reason supplied by legitimate authority and coercive prudence, but that ambiguity becomes a productive live issue rather than a disguised concession.

evidence.observation: Folley distinguishes objective value from an agent's reason to comply and concedes that a divine enforcer can align prudence with prescribed conduct.

finalResolution.rationale: Round each dimension's Pass A/Pass B mean, then calculate the move score mechanically.

moves.speaker: Philip Goff
moves.sourceExcerpt: David Hume has this idea that all fundamental life goals are on a par. Reason is the slave of the passions. I just think that can't be true. Imagine someone whose fundamental life goal is counting blades of grass, and they don't enjoy it, they get no pleasure from it. That's just their fundamental life goal.
moves.summary: Goff rejects Humean parity among ultimate goals and defends objective evaluative hierarchy without divine command.
moves.selectionRationale: The move introduces a non-command realist alternative, but the auto-caption lacks an explicit speaker label at this transition.

passA.rationale: Goff supplies an intuitive counterexample to Humean parity and thereby sketches a non-command evaluative hierarchy. The intuition is relevant but does not establish objectivity or explain its normative authority, and equating its evidentness with arithmetic is underargued. Speaker attribution follows a medium-confidence caption handoff.

evidence.excerpt: Imagine someone whose fundamental life goal is counting blades of grass, and they don't enjoy it ... That is a pointless, stupid way to live ... as opposed to scientific advancement, or curing cancer.

passB.rationale: The example gives moral realism an intuitive foothold and responds to the threat of preference parity. It does not supply a theory explaining the hierarchy or answer the stance objection beyond an appeal to evident seeming, so the public warrant remains limited. Confidence is medium because the caption transition and locked attribution are not audio-verified.

evidence.observation: Goff uses an unenjoyed grass-counting life to deny that all fundamental goals are evaluatively on a par.
Folley presses that the judgment is still made from a stance; Goff answers chiefly that the hierarchy seems as evident as arithmetic.

finalResolution.rationale: Round each dimension's Pass A/Pass B mean, then calculate the move score mechanically.

moves.speaker: Jessica Frazier
moves.sourceExcerpt: It means that God is just another authority who, regardless of whether he's moral or not, has got the power to decide for us what we ought to do, and we're going to defer to it. There's also a political, a human, a practical danger to this kind of ‘whatever he says is innately good because he says it.’
moves.summary: Frazier argues that sheer divine authority risks obedience to power and human appropriation of alleged commands.
moves.selectionRationale: This is the strongest direct objection to the qualified-authority bridge in Craig's command account.

passA.rationale: Frazier directly exposes the difference between justified authority and coercive power and adds a concrete epistemic-political risk: humans can appropriate alleged commands. But she partly answers Folley's enforcement framing rather than Craig's stated good-nature qualification, weakening charity. Speaker attribution follows a medium-confidence caption handoff.

evidence.excerpt: God is just another authority who, regardless of whether he's moral or not, has got the power to decide for us what we ought to do ... a political, a human, a practical danger.

passB.rationale: The practical warning about human appropriation of alleged commands is relevant and consequential. As a direct reply, however, the move substitutes sheer power and 'whatever he says' for Craig's explicit good-nature qualification, leaving the strongest pro version substantially unanswered. Confidence is medium because the caption transition and locked attribution are not audio-verified.

evidence.observation: Frazier warns that obedience to divine power can become servility and that humans may appropriate claimed authority.
Craig's actual account had made God's paradigmatic goodness, not power alone, the qualification for command.

adjudication.rationale: The warning about human appropriation of alleged commands is a consequential reply to public authority. But the move recasts Craig's explicitly good-nature-qualified account as sheer power and 'whatever he says,' leaving the strongest pro formulation only partly answered. The unresolved caption handoff also limits confidence.

finalResolution.rationale: The warning about human appropriation of alleged commands is a consequential reply to public authority. But the move recasts Craig's explicitly good-nature-qualified account as sheer power and 'whatever he says,' leaving the strongest pro formulation only partly answered. The unresolved caption handoff also limits confidence.

passA.rationale: A two-point full-debate adjustment records the consequential absence of a direct pro answer to Goff's adopted suffering-based challenge to classical divine power. That missing reply is not itself represented by a scored pro move; the underdevelopment of the enumerated arguments is already priced into S1-M1 and is not deducted again.

passB.rationale: The adjustment addresses consequential debate-wide omissions not fully represented by a selected reply: the classical package's suffering liability receives no sustained pro answer, and the motion-level inference to a personal classical creator remains incomplete beyond the listed arguments. The underdevelopment already reflected in S1-M1 is not penalized again.

final.rationale: Rounded mean of the two locked scoring passes; no adjudication threshold was triggered.

passA.rationale: A one-point full-debate adjustment records that Goff adopted a limited-God solution to suffering but did not explain the limitation or show that it predicts the observed scale and distribution of suffering. The thinner mechanisms in Frazier's and Folley's positive accounts are already reflected in their move scores and are not deducted again.

passB.rationale: The con side's strongest specifically theological alternative never explains the nature or degree of divine limitation or why it predicts the observed suffering. Other gaps in Frazier's and Folley's accounts are already reflected in their selected moves and are not counted again.

final.rationale: Rounded mean of the two locked scoring passes; no adjudication threshold was triggered.
